authoredSolutions.26: Reverse osmosis needs a genuinely semipermeable partition, so cellophane and parchment paper qualify while a merely porous partition lets solute through and does not. Chamber 1 holds the more concentrated solution \(\left(c_{1}>c_{2}\right)\), so solvent has to be driven OUT of chamber 1, which requires the pressure applied on chamber 1 to exceed the osmotic pressure, i.e. \(p_{1}>\pi\). Statement A (cellophane, \(p_{1}>\pi\)) and statement C (parchment paper, \(p_{1}>\pi\)) meet both requirements; B fails on the membrane and D pushes on the dilute side. Hence the correct choice is option (C), 'A and C only'.
authoredSolutions.27: Spontaneity requires \(\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S<0\). With both \(\Delta H>0\) and \(\Delta S>0\), the term \(-T\Delta S\) only overcomes the positive \(\Delta H\) at sufficiently high temperature. At equilibrium \(\Delta G=0\), which defines \(T_{e}=\Delta H/\Delta S\). Therefore \(\Delta G<0\) whenever \(T>\Delta H/\Delta S=T_{e}\), i.e. the reaction becomes spontaneous for \(T>T_{e}\), which is option (C).
authoredSolutions.28: The five in-stem structures are (A) \(O_{2}\), (B) \(N_{2}\), (C) \(F_{2}\), (D) \(S_{2}\) and (E) \(Cl_{2}\). In \(N_{2}\), \(F_{2}\) and \(Cl_{2}\) every molecular orbital is doubly occupied, so all three are diamagnetic. Only A and D are paramagnetic, giving option (D).

authoredSolutions.30: For an ideal gas at constant temperature the internal energy does not change, so \(\Delta U=0\). For a reversible isothermal expansion \(w=-nRT\ln\left(V_{2}/V_{1}\right)=-1\times 8.3\times 300\times \ln 2\). Using \(\ln 2=2.303\log 2=2.3\times 0.30=0.69\), \(w=-8.3\times 300\times 0.69=-1718\ J=-1.718\ kJ\). Since \(\Delta U=q+w=0\), the heat absorbed is \(q=-w=+1.718\ kJ\). Only option (D) carries the work value \(-1.718\ kJ\), so (D) is the answer.

authoredSolutions.101: P is a normal N-methyl six-membered lactam, in which the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the adjacent \(C=O\), so it is only weakly basic. authoredSolutions.102: Removing an electron from \(Mn^{2+}\) means breaking the stable half-filled \(3d^{5}\) configuration, which is unusually difficult, so the third ionisation enthalpy of manganese \(\left(3248\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\right)\) is HIGHER than that of iron \(\left(2957\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\right)\), whose \(Fe^{2+}\) is \(3d^{6}\).
